# How to use this guide

* **Exam format:** 30–35 multiple-choice questions, choices a–e. You get a periodic table. **You do not get the
  solubility rules, so memorize Table 7.1** (Section 7.3).
* **Mix:** expect about half concept questions (definitions, classifications, "which is true") and half calculations.
* Each section lists the slides it comes from (`Chapter N post.pdf` / `.pptx`, same slide numbers). **Definitions are
  in the course's wording.** When a textbook or website words something differently, go with the slides.
* Every "Worked example" is a practice problem from the slides, solved step by step. Cover the solution, try it, then check.
* After each practice exam, use its key's "Source" line to jump back to the matching section here.

# Chapter 7 — Reactions in Aqueous Solutions

## 7.1 Driving forces (Ch 7 slides 2–4)

A reaction tends to happen when it forms one of these. Memorize all four.

1. **Formation of a solid** (precipitation)
2. **Formation of water** (acid–base)
3. **Transfer of electrons** (oxidation–reduction)
4. **Formation of a gas** (gas evolution)

## 7.2 Ions in water and electrolytes (Ch 7 slides 6–10)

* When an ionic solid dissolves, **the ions separate and move around independently**. Ba(NO~3~)~2~(aq) contains
  separated Ba^2+^ and NO~3~^−^ ions (two NO~3~^−^ for every Ba^2+^), not Ba(NO~3~)~2~ units.
* Pure water does **not** conduct electricity. Ions must be present for current to flow.
* **Strong electrolyte:** a substance where every unit that dissolves produces separated ions.
* **A solid compound must have zero net charge**, so a precipitate must contain both a cation and an anion. Two cations
  (K^+^ and Ba^2+^) or two anions (CrO~4~^2−^ and NO~3~^−^) can never form a solid together (slide 10).

## 7.3 Solubility rules — MEMORIZE (Ch 7 slide 11, Table 7.1)

| # | Rule | Exceptions to know |
|:-:|:--|:--|
| 1 | Most **nitrate** (NO~3~^−^) salts are **soluble** | — |
| 2 | Most salts of **Na^+^, K^+^, NH~4~^+^** are **soluble** | — |
| 3 | Most **chloride** salts are **soluble** | **AgCl, PbCl~2~, Hg~2~Cl~2~** are insoluble |
| 4 | Most **sulfate** salts are **soluble** | **BaSO~4~, PbSO~4~, CaSO~4~** are insoluble |
| 5 | Most **hydroxides** are only **slightly soluble** | **NaOH, KOH** soluble; Ba(OH)~2~, Ca(OH)~2~ moderately soluble |
| 6 | Most **sulfide** (S^2−^), **carbonate** (CO~3~^2−^), **phosphate** (PO~4~^3−^) salts are only **slightly soluble** | — |

"Insoluble" and "slightly soluble" mean the same thing here: too little dissolves to see.

**Rules 1 and 2 beat rules 5 and 6.** If a compound contains Na^+^, K^+^, NH~4~^+^, or NO~3~^−^, it is soluble, even when
the other ion is a sulfide, carbonate, phosphate, or hydroxide. Examples: (NH~4~)~2~S, K~3~PO~4~, and Na~2~CO~3~ are all **soluble**.

Memory aid, in three tiers:

* **Always soluble:** NO~3~^−^, Na^+^, K^+^, NH~4~^+^.
* **Soluble except:** Cl^−^ (except **Ag, Pb, Hg~2~**), SO~4~^2−^ (except **Ba, Pb, Ca**). Pb is on both exception lists.
* **Insoluble except tier 1:** OH^−^ (NaOH, KOH soluble), S^2−^, CO~3~^2−^, PO~4~^3−^.

**Worked example (slide 12).** Classify NaOH, BaSO~4~, CaCO~3~.

* NaOH: **soluble**. It is a named exception in rule 5, and rule 2 covers Na^+^.
* BaSO~4~: **insoluble**. It is a named exception in rule 4.
* CaCO~3~: **insoluble**. Rule 6 covers carbonates, and Ca^2+^ is not a rule-2 cation.

**HW14 style:** "Which rule explains why ammonium sulfide is soluble?" Answer: *most salts of NH~4~^+^ are soluble* (rule 2),
**not** the sulfide rule.

## 7.4 Predicting precipitates (Ch 7 slide 14)

1. **Write the reactants as they actually exist** (separated ions).
2. **Consider the solids that could form** by **exchanging the anions**.
3. **Use the solubility rules** to decide whether either product is insoluble. If neither is, write **NR** (no reaction).

**Worked example (slides 15–17).** K~2~CrO~4~(aq) + Ba(NO~3~)~2~(aq).
The ions are K^+^, CrO~4~^2−^, Ba^2+^, NO~3~^−^. Swapping anions gives KNO~3~ (soluble, rules 1 and 2) and BaCrO~4~,
which is the solid on the slides.

$$\text{K}_2\text{CrO}_4(aq) + \text{Ba(NO}_3)_2(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaCrO}_4(s) + 2\text{KNO}_3(aq)$$

**NR example (HW15).** KNO~3~(aq) + Na~2~S(aq). Swapping gives K~2~S and NaNO~3~. Both contain rule-2 cations, so both are
soluble and the answer is **NR**.

## 7.5 Three kinds of equations (Ch 7 slides 15–20)

| Equation | Shows | Spectator ions? |
|:--|:--|:-:|
| **Molecular** | complete formulas of all reactants and products; doesn't show the actual forms in solution | n/a |
| **Complete ionic** | every **strong electrolyte** written as separated ions; **all** reactants and products included | included |
| **Net ionic** | **only the components that undergo a change** (are directly involved) | **left out** |

* **Spectator ions:** ions that don't participate directly in the reaction. They appear unchanged on both sides.
* Write as ions: soluble ionic compounds (aq), strong acids, strong bases. Keep as full formulas: solids (s), water (l),
  gases (g), and weak acids such as HNO~2~.

**Worked example (slide 19).** Pb(NO~3~)~2~(aq) + 2KI(aq) $\rightarrow$ PbI~2~(s) + 2KNO~3~(aq)

* Complete ionic: Pb^2+^(aq) + 2NO~3~^−^(aq) + 2K^+^(aq) + 2I^−^(aq) $\rightarrow$ PbI~2~(s) + 2K^+^(aq) + 2NO~3~^−^(aq)
* Cancel the spectators K^+^ and NO~3~^−^.
* Net ionic: **Pb^2+^(aq) + 2I^−^(aq) $\rightarrow$ PbI~2~(s)**

**Worked example (slide 20).** Sodium chloride solution added to silver nitrate solution.

* Molecular: NaCl(aq) + AgNO~3~(aq) $\rightarrow$ AgCl(s) + NaNO~3~(aq). AgCl is a rule-3 exception.
* Complete ionic: Na^+^(aq) + Cl^−^(aq) + Ag^+^(aq) + NO~3~^−^(aq) $\rightarrow$ AgCl(s) + Na^+^(aq) + NO~3~^−^(aq)
* Net ionic: **Ag^+^(aq) + Cl^−^(aq) $\rightarrow$ AgCl(s)**

**Net ionic checklist:** right states, the smallest whole-number coefficients, and both charge and atoms balanced.

## 7.6 Acids, bases, and acid–base reactions (Ch 7 slides 21–28)

**Course definitions**

* **Arrhenius acid:** a substance that produces **H^+^ ions** (protons) when dissolved in water.
* **Arrhenius base:** a substance that produces **hydroxide ions (OH^−^)** in water.
* **Strong acid:** a substance that **completely dissociates (ionizes)** in water. Each molecule breaks into H^+^ plus an anion.
  Because strong acids are strong electrolytes that produce H^+^, they are called strong acids.
* **Strong base:** a **metal hydroxide that is very soluble in water** and completely breaks up into separated ions.
  Strong bases are **strong electrolytes**.
* **Salt:** the ionic compound formed along with water in an acid–base reaction. It may stay dissolved or precipitate.

**Memorize the lists:**

* **Strong acids: HCl, HNO~3~, H~2~SO~4~.** Anything else here (HNO~2~, HF, HC~2~H~3~O~2~, H~3~PO~4~) is not on the list.
* **Strong bases: NaOH, KOH.** (HW16 also uses CsOH, another very soluble group-1 hydroxide.)

**The six principles (slides 24–26), condensed**

1. The common strong acids are HCl, HNO~3~, H~2~SO~4~.
2. A strong acid completely dissociates.
3. A strong base is a very soluble metal hydroxide (NaOH, KOH) that completely breaks into ions.
4. **Strong acid + strong base always has the same net ionic equation: H^+^(aq) + OH^−^(aq) $\rightarrow$ H~2~O(l).**
5. One product is always water. The other is a **salt** that stays dissolved and can be recovered by evaporating the water.
6. H^+^ is the acidic ion and OH^−^ is the basic ion.

**Naming the salt (HW16):** the base's cation goes with the acid's anion. HI + NaOH gives **NaI**, NaOH + HNO~3~ gives
**NaNO~3~**, and HCl + CsOH gives **CsCl**.

**Worked example (slide 27).** Balance H~3~PO~4~ + Ca(OH)~2~ $\rightarrow$ Ca~3~(PO~4~)~2~ + H~2~O.

1. Balance Ca: 3 Ca(OH)~2~.
2. Balance PO~4~ as a unit: 2 H~3~PO~4~.
3. Balance H and O: 6 H^+^ + 6 OH^−^ make 6 H~2~O.

$$2\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4 + 3\text{Ca(OH)}_2 \rightarrow \text{Ca}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2(s) + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

Ca~3~(PO~4~)~2~ is a phosphate (rule 6), so it precipitates. Phosphoric acid isn't on the strong-acid list, so leave it
molecular in the ionic equations:

* Net ionic: 2H~3~PO~4~(aq) + 3Ca^2+^(aq) + 6OH^−^(aq) $\rightarrow$ Ca~3~(PO~4~)~2~(s) + 6H~2~O(l)

**Worked example (slide 28).** Nitrous acid + potassium hydroxide.

* Molecular: HNO~2~(aq) + KOH(aq) $\rightarrow$ KNO~2~(aq) + H~2~O(l), which is already balanced.
* HNO~2~ is not a strong acid, so it stays molecular. KOH and KNO~2~ are written as ions.
* Complete ionic: HNO~2~(aq) + K^+^(aq) + OH^−^(aq) $\rightarrow$ K^+^(aq) + NO~2~^−^(aq) + H~2~O(l)
* Net ionic: **HNO~2~(aq) + OH^−^(aq) $\rightarrow$ NO~2~^−^(aq) + H~2~O(l)**. Only a **strong** acid gives H^+^ + OH^−^ $\rightarrow$ H~2~O.

## 7.7 Oxidation–reduction (Ch 7 slides 29–34, 38)

* **Oxidation–reduction (redox) reaction:** a reaction that involves a **transfer of electrons**. One species loses electrons
  and another gains them (HW16).
* **Principle 1:** **metal + nonmetal always makes an ionic compound and is always redox.** The metal loses electrons to become
  a cation, and the nonmetal gains them to become an anion.
* **Principle 2:** two nonmetals can also undergo redox. **For now, you recognize these by O~2~ appearing as a reactant or
  product.** The compound formed by two nonmetals is not ionic.

**How many electrons?** Use the charges in the ionic product. The number of electrons lost per metal atom equals the cation's charge.

| Reaction | Ions formed | Electrons |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 2Li + F~2~ $\rightarrow$ 2LiF (slide 38) | Li^+^, F^−^ | each Li loses 1; each F gains 1 |
| Ba + Cl~2~ $\rightarrow$ BaCl~2~ (HW16) | Ba^2+^, Cl^−^ | Ba loses 2; Cl~2~ gains 2 (1 per Cl) |
| **2Al + N~2~ $\rightarrow$ 2AlN (slide 33)** | Al^3+^, N^3−^ | **each Al loses 3**; each N gains 3 |

**Worked example (slide 34).** Solid copper reacts with aqueous iron(II) chloride to form solid iron and aqueous copper(II) chloride.

$$\text{Cu}(s) + \text{FeCl}_2(aq) \rightarrow \text{Fe}(s) + \text{CuCl}_2(aq)$$

This is already balanced. Cu (0) becomes Cu^2+^, so **Cu loses 2 e^−^**. Fe^2+^ becomes Fe (0), so **Fe^2+^ gains 2 e^−^**.
Cl^−^ doesn't change; it is a spectator.

## 7.8 Classifying reactions (Ch 7 slides 35–45)

| Class | How to spot it | Slide example |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Precipitation** | two solutions make a **solid** | K~2~CrO~4~ + Ba(NO~3~)~2~ $\rightarrow$ BaCrO~4~(s) + 2KNO~3~ |
| **Double-displacement** (double-exchange) | two anions **swap** partners | same as above |
| **Acid–base** | H^+^ ends up in **water** | HCl + KOH $\rightarrow$ H~2~O + KCl |
| **Oxidation–reduction** | **electrons transferred** (metal + nonmetal, or O~2~ involved) | 2Li + F~2~ $\rightarrow$ 2LiF |
| **Gas evolution** | a **gas** forms (also acid–base here) | 2HCl + Na~2~CO~3~ $\rightarrow$ CO~2~(g) + H~2~O + 2NaCl |
| **Single-replacement** | **one** anion moves from one cation to another (always redox) | Zn + 2HCl $\rightarrow$ ZnCl~2~ + H~2~ |
| **Combustion** | reacts with **oxygen**, releasing energy so fast that a **flame** results | CH~4~ + 2O~2~ $\rightarrow$ CO~2~ + 2H~2~O |
| **Synthesis** (combination) | a compound forms from **simpler materials** | 2Na + Cl~2~ $\rightarrow$ 2NaCl |
| **Decomposition** | a compound breaks into simpler compounds or elements, usually by **heat or electric current** | 2HgO $\rightarrow$ 2Hg + O~2~ |

**One reaction can belong to several classes** (HW17):

* C + O~2~ $\rightarrow$ CO~2~ is synthesis, combustion, and redox.
* 2Fe + 3Cl~2~ $\rightarrow$ 2FeCl~3~ is synthesis and redox, but **not** combustion (no O~2~).
* Combustion and synthesis/decomposition with elements are all redox. Combustion also produces **heat/energy** (HW17).

**Worked example (slide 44).**

* N~2~ + 3H~2~ $\rightarrow$ 2NH~3~ is **synthesis**.
* C~6~H~12~O~6~ + 6O~2~ $\rightarrow$ 6CO~2~ + 6H~2~O is **combustion**.
* 2H~2~O $\rightarrow$ 2H~2~ + O~2~ is **decomposition**.

**Balancing from words (HW17):**

* Phosphorus + chlorine: P~4~ + 6Cl~2~ $\rightarrow$ 4PCl~3~
* Ammonium nitrite decomposes: NH~4~NO~2~ $\rightarrow$ N~2~ + 2H~2~O
* Hydrobromic acid decomposes: 2HBr $\rightarrow$ H~2~ + Br~2~

# Chapter 8 — Chemical Composition

## 8.1 Counting by weighing; atomic mass units (Ch 8 slides 2–6)

* Objects that differ slightly can be **counted by weighing** if you know their **average mass** (the jellybean idea).
* **Atomic mass unit (slide 5):** a tiny unit of mass made for weighing single atoms. 1 amu = 1.66 × 10^−24^ g.
* **Average atomic mass (Table 8.1):** the mass of **ONE atom** of the element, in **amu**. It is an *average* only because
  an element's atoms are a mix of isotopes with slightly different masses (like jellybeans of slightly different sizes), so
  the number is the mass of a typical single atom. Table 8.1: H 1.008 amu, C 12.01 amu, N 14.01 amu, O 16.00 amu,
  Na 22.99 amu, Al 26.98 amu.

| Number from the periodic table (C: 12.01) read as | Means | Unit |
|:--|:--|:-:|
| Average atomic mass | mass of **1 carbon atom** | **amu** |
| Molar mass (section 8.2) | mass of **1 mole** (6.022 × 10^23^) of carbon atoms | **g/mol** |

**Mass of one atom in grams:** multiply its amu value by 1.66 × 10^−24^ g/amu.

$$1\ \text{C atom} = 12.01\ \text{amu}\times\frac{1.66\times10^{-24}\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{amu}} = 1.99\times10^{-23}\ \text{g}$$

Check that the two readings agree: 6.022 × 10^23^ atoms × 1.99 × 10^−23^ g per atom = 12.0 g, so one mole of carbon weighs
12.01 g. That's why the same number serves as amu per atom and as grams per mole.

* **Key idea (slide 6):** samples whose masses are in the **same ratio as their atomic masses** contain the **same number of
  atoms**. So 26.98 g Al and 63.55 g Cu contain the same number of atoms.

## 8.2 The mole (Ch 8 slides 7–9)

* **Mole (course definition):** the number equal to the number of carbon atoms in **12.01 g of carbon**.
* **Avogadro's number:** 6.022 × 10^23^. One mole of anything is 6.022 × 10^23^ units of it.
* 1 mol of any element has a mass in grams equal to its atomic mass (Table 8.2): Al 26.98 g, Au 196.97 g, Fe 55.85 g,
  S 32.07 g, B 10.81 g, Xe 131.3 g, and every one of these contains 6.022 × 10^23^ atoms.

## 8.3 The conversion map (Ch 8 slides 10–15)

$$\text{grams} \;\xrightarrow{\;\div\ \text{molar mass}\;}\; \text{moles} \;\xrightarrow{\;\times\ 6.022\times10^{23}\;}\; \text{atoms or molecules}$$

Go backward by doing the opposite operations. **Moles are always the middle step.** For mg, $\mu$g, or kg, convert to grams first.

The two conversion factors on this map:

| Factor | Converts | Where the number comes from |
|:--|:--|:--|
| $\dfrac{1\ \text{mol X}}{\text{atomic mass of X in g}}$ (or flipped) | grams $\leftrightarrow$ moles | The element's atomic mass on the periodic table, read as **g/mol** (section 8.1) |
| $\dfrac{6.022\times10^{23}\ \text{atoms}}{1\ \text{mol}}$ (or flipped) | moles $\leftrightarrow$ atoms | Avogadro's number: 1 mol is always 6.022 × 10^23^ things (section 8.2) |

Put the unit you **want** on top and the unit you **have** on the bottom so the old unit cancels.

**Worked example (slide 10).** How many H atoms are in 0.500 g of H?

*Step 1: grams to moles.* The atomic mass of H is 1.008, so 1 mol H weighs 1.008 g. You have grams, so grams goes on the bottom:

$$0.500\ \cancel{\text{g H}}\times\underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol H}}{1.008\ \cancel{\text{g H}}}}_{\text{atomic mass of H}} = 0.496\ \text{mol H}$$

*Step 2: moles to atoms.* 1 mol is 6.022 × 10^23^ atoms. You have moles, so moles goes on the bottom:

$$0.496\ \cancel{\text{mol H}}\times\underbrace{\frac{6.022\times10^{23}\ \text{H atoms}}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol H}}}}_{\text{Avogadro's number}} = \mathbf{2.99\times10^{23}\ H\ atoms}$$

**Worked example (slide 11).** 3.60 g Al to moles. The atomic mass of Al is 26.98, so 1 mol Al = 26.98 g:

$$3.60\ \cancel{\text{g Al}}\times\underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol Al}}{26.98\ \cancel{\text{g Al}}}}_{\text{atomic mass of Al}} = \mathbf{0.133\ mol\ Al}$$

**Worked example (slide 12).** 544 g Ca to moles. The atomic mass of Ca is 40.08:

$$544\ \cancel{\text{g Ca}}\times\underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol Ca}}{40.08\ \cancel{\text{g Ca}}}}_{\text{atomic mass of Ca}} = \mathbf{13.6\ mol\ Ca}$$

**Worked example (slide 13).** 0.133 mol Al (from slide 11) to atoms:

$$0.133\ \cancel{\text{mol Al}}\times\underbrace{\frac{6.022\times10^{23}\ \text{Al atoms}}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol Al}}}}_{\text{Avogadro's number}} = \mathbf{8.01\times10^{22}\ Al\ atoms}$$

**Worked example (slide 14).** 13.6 mol Ca (from slide 12) to atoms:

$$13.6\ \cancel{\text{mol Ca}}\times\underbrace{\frac{6.022\times10^{23}\ \text{Ca atoms}}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol Ca}}}}_{\text{Avogadro's number}} = \mathbf{8.19\times10^{24}\ Ca\ atoms}$$

**Worked example (slide 15): going backward, atoms to grams.** What is the mass of 2.31 × 10^22^ Au atoms?
Atoms to moles uses Avogadro's number **flipped** (atoms on the bottom), then moles to grams uses the atomic mass of Au
(196.97) **with grams on top**:

$$2.31\times10^{22}\ \cancel{\text{Au atoms}}\times\underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol Au}}{6.022\times10^{23}\ \cancel{\text{Au atoms}}}}_{\text{Avogadro's number, flipped}} = 0.0384\ \text{mol Au}$$

$$0.0384\ \cancel{\text{mol Au}}\times\underbrace{\frac{196.97\ \text{g Au}}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol Au}}}}_{\text{atomic mass of Au}} = \mathbf{7.56\ g\ Au}$$

**Reality check (slide 19):** a sample smaller than 1 molar mass must be less than 1 mol and fewer than 6.022 × 10^23^ atoms.
An atom count around 10^−20^ or 10^50^ means you flipped a factor upside down.

**HW18 style:** "A sample of Co contains 3.10 × 10^24^ atoms; a sample of Mn contains 4.10 mol. Which has more atoms?"
You can only compare amounts in the same unit, so convert the Mn to atoms:

$$4.10\ \cancel{\text{mol Mn}}\times\underbrace{\frac{6.022\times10^{23}\ \text{Mn atoms}}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol Mn}}}}_{\text{Avogadro's number}} = 2.47\times10^{24}\ \text{Mn atoms}$$

3.10 × 10^24^ Co atoms is more than 2.47 × 10^24^ Mn atoms, so the **Co** sample has more atoms.

## 8.4 Conceptual problem solving (Ch 8 slides 16–19)

1. **Where are we going?** Read the problem, identify the final goal, and sort the facts given (draw it if it helps).
2. **How do we get there?** Work backward from the goal. In stoichiometry, always start with the balanced equation.
3. **Reality check:** does the answer make sense?

## 8.5 Molar mass (Ch 8 slides 21–29)

* **Molar mass:** the mass in grams of **1 mole** of a substance, found by **summing the masses of the component atoms**.
* **A subscript outside parentheses multiplies everything inside.** Ba(OH)~2~ has 1 Ba, 2 O, and 2 H.

**How to calculate one:** (1) count how many atoms of each element are in the formula (the subscript; no subscript means 1);
(2) multiply each count by that element's atomic mass from the periodic table; (3) add the results.

**Worked examples.** Each term is (number of atoms) × (atomic mass of that element).

| Slide | Compound | Atom count | (count × atomic mass), added | Molar mass |
|:-:|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 22 | CH~4~ | 1 C, 4 H | 1(12.01) + 4(1.008) | **16.04 g/mol** |
| 23 | NH~3~ | 1 N, 3 H | 1(14.01) + 3(1.008) | **17.03 g/mol** |
| 24 | H~2~SO~4~ | 2 H, 1 S, 4 O | 2(1.008) + 1(32.07) + 4(16.00) | **98.09 g/mol** |
| 25 | C~6~H~12~O~6~ | 6 C, 12 H, 6 O | 6(12.01) + 12(1.008) + 6(16.00) | **180.16 g/mol** |
| 26 | Ba(OH)~2~ | 1 Ba, 2 O, 2 H | 1(137.33) + 2(16.00) + 2(1.008) | **171.35 g/mol** |

**Mass and moles (slides 27–29).** The molar mass is the conversion factor: 1 mol of the compound = (molar mass) g.

**Slide 27.** What is the mass of 7.89 mol NaOH? Molar mass of NaOH = 22.99 + 16.00 + 1.008 = 40.00 g/mol. You have moles
and want grams, so grams goes on top:

$$7.89\ \cancel{\text{mol NaOH}}\times\underbrace{\frac{40.00\ \text{g NaOH}}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol NaOH}}}}_{\text{molar mass of NaOH}} = \mathbf{316\ g\ NaOH}$$

**Slide 28.** How many moles are in 982 g FeO? Molar mass of FeO = 55.85 + 16.00 = 71.85 g/mol. You have grams and want
moles, so grams goes on the bottom:

$$982\ \cancel{\text{g FeO}}\times\underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol FeO}}{71.85\ \cancel{\text{g FeO}}}}_{\text{molar mass of FeO}} = \mathbf{13.7\ mol\ FeO}$$

**Slide 29.** How many moles are in 9.43 mg CaCl~2~? Molar mass of CaCl~2~ = 40.08 + 2(35.45) = 110.98 g/mol. The molar
mass is in **grams**, so convert mg to g first (1 g = 1000 mg):

$$9.43\ \cancel{\text{mg}}\times\underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{g}}{1000\ \cancel{\text{mg}}}}_{\text{metric}} = 9.43\times10^{-3}\ \text{g CaCl}_2$$

$$9.43\times10^{-3}\ \cancel{\text{g CaCl}_2}\times\underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol CaCl}_2}{110.98\ \cancel{\text{g CaCl}_2}}}_{\text{molar mass of CaCl}_2} = \mathbf{8.50\times10^{-5}\ mol}$$

**HW19 style: name to formula to molar mass.** Write the formula first, then add up its atoms. Iron(II) chloride = FeCl~2~:
55.85 + 2(35.45) = **126.75 g/mol**. Copper(II) sulfate = CuSO~4~: 63.55 + 32.07 + 4(16.00) = **159.62 g/mol**.
Rubidium chloride = RbCl.

**HW19 style: moles of an atom to molecules.** "A sample of C~6~H~6~ contains 5.09 mol C. How many C~6~H~6~ molecules
are there?" Each C~6~H~6~ molecule contains **6** C atoms (the subscript), so 1 mol C~6~H~6~ contains 6 mol C. Use
that as the factor, then Avogadro's number:

$$5.09\ \cancel{\text{mol C}}\times\underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol C}_6\text{H}_6}{6\ \cancel{\text{mol C}}}}_{\text{subscript of C in C}_6\text{H}_6} = 0.848\ \text{mol C}_6\text{H}_6$$

$$0.848\ \cancel{\text{mol}}\times\underbrace{\frac{6.022\times10^{23}\ \text{molecules}}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol}}}}_{\text{Avogadro's number}} = \mathbf{5.11\times10^{23}\ molecules}$$

## 8.6 Mass percent (Ch 8 slides 30–33)

$$\text{mass percent of element} = \frac{\text{mass of the element in 1 mol of compound}}{\text{mass of 1 mol of compound}}\times100\%$$

**Method:** (1) find the molar mass of the compound (section 8.5). (2) For each element, the top of the fraction is
(number of that atom in the formula) × (its atomic mass). (3) Divide by the molar mass and multiply by 100.

**Worked example (slide 31).** Ethanol, C~2~H~5~OH. Count the atoms: 2 C, **6** H (5 + the 1 in OH), 1 O.
Molar mass = 2(12.01) + 6(1.008) + 1(16.00) = 24.02 + 6.048 + 16.00 = 46.07 g/mol.

* C: $\dfrac{2(12.01) = 24.02\ \text{g C}}{46.07\ \text{g C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}}\times100\% =$ **52.14%**
* H: $\dfrac{6(1.008) = 6.048\ \text{g H}}{46.07\ \text{g C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}}\times100\% =$ **13.13%**
* O: $\dfrac{1(16.00) = 16.00\ \text{g O}}{46.07\ \text{g C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}}\times100\% =$ **34.73%**

These add to 100%, which checks the work.

**Worked example (slide 32).** H~3~PO~4~: 3 H, 1 P, 4 O. Molar mass = 3(1.008) + 30.97 + 4(16.00) = 97.99 g/mol.

* H: 3(1.008) = 3.024 g; 3.024 / 97.99 × 100 = **3.09%**
* P: 1(30.97) = 30.97 g; 30.97 / 97.99 × 100 = **31.60%**
* O: 4(16.00) = 64.00 g; 64.00 / 97.99 × 100 = **65.31%**

**Worked example (slide 33).** Magnesium iodite, Mg(IO~2~)~2~ (the iodite ion is IO~2~^−^). The subscript 2 outside the
parentheses doubles everything inside, so there are 1 Mg, **2** I, and **4** O.
Molar mass = 24.31 + 2(126.90) + 4(16.00) = 342.11 g/mol.

* Mg: 1(24.31) = 24.31 g; 24.31 / 342.11 × 100 = **7.11%**
* I: 2(126.90) = 253.80 g; 253.80 / 342.11 × 100 = **74.19%**
* O: 4(16.00) = 64.00 g; 64.00 / 342.11 × 100 = **18.71%**

**Trap:** count the atoms of that element in the formula. KNO~2~ has 2 O, and PCl~5~ has 5 Cl (HW20: P 14.87%, Cl 85.13%).

## 8.7 Empirical and molecular formulas (Ch 8 slides 34–50)

### Definitions

* **Empirical (simplest) formula:** the **smallest whole-number ratio** of atoms in the compound.
* **Molecular formula:** the **actual** formula: how many of each atom are really in one molecule.
* **Molecular formula = (empirical formula)~n~**, where n is a whole number (1, 2, 3, ...).
  Glucose is C~6~H~12~O~6~. Divide every subscript by 6 to get its empirical formula, CH~2~O, so n = 6.
* **What data you need (slide 47, HW21):** the empirical formula needs the **composition by mass**. The molecular formula
  needs the composition **and the molar mass**.

There are **three different problem types** in this section. Figure out which one you have before you start.

| You are given | You are asked for | Use |
|:--|:--|:--|
| A molecular formula (e.g. C~4~H~8~O~2~) | The empirical formula | **Type A**: reduce the subscripts. No masses needed. |
| Masses or mass percents of each element | The empirical formula | **Type B**: the 4-step mass $\rightarrow$ moles method |
| An empirical formula and a molar mass | The molecular formula | **Type C**: find n |

### Type A: molecular formula $\rightarrow$ empirical formula (slide 40)

You already have the atom counts, so **skip the mass and mole steps entirely**. Find the largest number that divides
evenly into **every** subscript, and divide every subscript by it. A subscript you can't see is 1.

| Molecular formula | Subscripts | Largest number dividing all of them | Empirical formula |
|:--|:--|:-:|:--|
| H~2~O~2~ | H 2, O 2 | 2 | **HO** |
| C~4~H~8~O~2~ | C 4, H 8, O 2 | 2 | **C~2~H~4~O** |
| P~4~O~10~ | P 4, O 10 | 2 | **P~2~O~5~** |
| C~6~H~12~O~6~ | C 6, H 12, O 6 | 6 | **CH~2~O** |
| C~7~H~6~O~2~ (benzoic acid, HW20) | C 7, H 6, O 2 | 1 (nothing divides 7, 6, and 2) | **C~7~H~6~O~2~**, unchanged |

If the only number that divides every subscript is 1, the formula is **already empirical**.

### Type B: masses or percents $\rightarrow$ empirical formula (slides 35–37, 42–46)

You only know **how many grams** of each element there are. A formula counts **atoms**, so first convert grams to moles,
then compare the moles.

**Step 1: Get grams of each element.**
If you're given percents, pretend you have **exactly 100 g** of the compound. Then each percent is that many grams:
32.0% C becomes 32.0 g C. If you're given grams, use them as they are.

**Step 2: Convert each element's grams to moles.** Do this separately for each element, using that element's atomic mass
from the periodic table:

$$\text{mol of element} = \frac{\text{grams of that element}}{\text{atomic mass of that element (g/mol)}}$$

**Step 3: Divide every mole value by the smallest mole value.**
Look at the moles from step 2 and find the **smallest** one. Then divide **each** element's moles, including the smallest
itself, by that one number. The smallest always becomes exactly 1, and the others tell you how many of that atom there
are per 1 of the smallest.

**Step 4: Turn the step-3 results into whole-number subscripts.**

* **"Whole number" means within about 0.1 of an integer.** Measured data and rounded atomic masses add a little error, so
  1.997, 2.03, and 0.98 all count as whole: round them to 2, 2, and 1.
* If a result ends in one of the decimals below, **don't round it**. It's a real fraction, so multiply.
* **Pick ONE multiplier and multiply EVERY element's result by it**, including the ones that were already whole. Use the
  smallest multiplier that makes **all** of them whole at the same time. (Using a different multiplier for each element
  would change the ratio and give a wrong formula.)

| Decimal part of a step-3 result | Meaning | Multiply **every** result by |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| about .5 | halves | **2** |
| about .33 or .67 | thirds | **3** |
| about .25 or .75 | quarters | **4** |
| about .2, .4, .6, or .8 | fifths | **5** |

If two elements need different multipliers, use the smallest number that works for both. For example, a .5 and a .33
together need 6.

The final whole numbers are the subscripts.

**Worked example A, all whole after step 3 (slide 38).** C 9.94%, Cl 58.6%, F 31.4%.

| Element | Step 1: g (100 g sample) | Step 2: mol = g ÷ atomic mass | Step 3: ÷ smallest (0.828) | Step 4 |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| C | 9.94 | 9.94 ÷ 12.01 = 0.828 | 0.828 ÷ 0.828 = 1.00 | 1 |
| Cl | 58.6 | 58.6 ÷ 35.45 = 1.653 | 1.653 ÷ 0.828 = 1.997 | 2 |
| F | 31.4 | 31.4 ÷ 19.00 = 1.653 | 1.653 ÷ 0.828 = 1.997 | 2 |

1.997 is within 0.1 of 2, so round it. No multiplying is needed. The empirical formula is **CCl~2~F~2~**.

**Worked example B, a .5 forces ×2.** An iron oxide is 69.94% Fe and 30.06% O.

| Element | Step 1: g | Step 2: mol | Step 3: ÷ smallest (1.252) | Step 4: × 2 |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| Fe | 69.94 | 69.94 ÷ 55.85 = 1.252 | 1.00 | 1.00 × 2 = **2** |
| O | 30.06 | 30.06 ÷ 16.00 = 1.879 | 1.50 | 1.50 × 2 = **3** |

1.50 is not within 0.1 of a whole number, and it ends in .5, so multiply **both** results by 2. The formula is **Fe~2~O~3~**.
Rounding 1.5 to 2 instead would give FeO~2~, which is wrong.

**Worked example C, a .33 forces ×3, applied to all three elements.** Vitamin C is 40.92% C, 4.58% H, 54.50% O.

| Element | Step 1: g | Step 2: mol | Step 3: ÷ smallest (3.406) | Step 4: × 3 |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| C | 40.92 | 40.92 ÷ 12.01 = 3.407 | 1.00 | **3** |
| H | 4.58 | 4.58 ÷ 1.008 = 4.544 | 1.334 | 4.00, so **4** |
| O | 54.50 | 54.50 ÷ 16.00 = 3.406 | 1.00 | **3** |

Only H came out as a fraction, but C and O get multiplied by 3 too, because the ratio has to stay the same. The empirical formula
is **C~3~H~4~O~3~**. Writing CH~4~O, with only H multiplied, is the classic mistake.

**Worked example D, starting from grams (slides 45–46).** 1.198 g C combines with 0.302 g H.

| Element | Step 1: g | Step 2: mol | Step 3: ÷ smallest (0.0998) | Step 4 |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| C | 1.198 | 1.198 ÷ 12.01 = 0.0998 | 1.00 | 1 |
| H | 0.302 | 0.302 ÷ 1.008 = 0.300 | 3.00 | 3 |

The empirical formula is **CH~3~**. You were given grams, so step 1 is just "use the given grams".

**Worked example E, four elements (slides 35–37).** 32.000% C, 6.714% H, 42.630% O, 18.660% N.
The moles are C 2.664, H 6.648, O 2.664, N 1.333. The smallest is 1.333, and dividing each by it gives 2, 5, 2, 1, so the formula is
**C~2~H~5~O~2~N**.

**HW21 style:** Mg 20.19%, S 26.64%, O 53.17% gives **MgSO~4~**. Si 10.85%, Cl 27.40%, Br 61.75% gives **SiCl~2~Br~2~**.
Work them with the same table to check yourself.

**Combustion analysis (slide 44):** a carbon-containing sample is burned in excess O~2~. The masses of the products give the
percent of C (and the other elements), and from there it's a Type B problem.

### Type C: empirical formula + molar mass $\rightarrow$ molecular formula (slides 47–49)

1. Add up the **empirical formula mass** (the molar mass of the empirical formula).
2. Divide: $n = \dfrac{\text{molar mass of the compound}}{\text{empirical formula mass}}$. The answer will be very close to a whole number.
3. **Multiply every subscript in the empirical formula by n.**

**Worked example (slide 49).** Empirical formula C~4~H~5~N~2~O, molar mass 194.14 g/mol.

1. Empirical mass = 4(12.01) + 5(1.008) + 2(14.01) + 16.00 = 97.10 g/mol.
2. n = 194.14 ÷ 97.10 = 2.00
3. C~4×2~H~5×2~N~2×2~O~1×2~ = **C~8~H~10~N~4~O~2~** (caffeine)

**HW21 style:**

* CH with molar mass about 26: CH = 13.02, n = 2, so **C~2~H~2~**.
* C~3~H~7~NO with molar mass 145–150: empirical mass 73.10, n = 2, so **C~6~H~14~N~2~O~2~**.
* Vitamin C from example C, C~3~H~4~O~3~ (88.06) with molar mass 176.12: n = 2, so **C~6~H~8~O~6~**.

**Why the molecular formula is more useful (slide 50):** it gives the actual number of atoms in a molecule. The empirical
formula only gives the ratio, and many different compounds share one empirical formula (C~2~H~2~ and C~6~H~6~ are both CH).

### Empirical-formula mistakes to avoid

1. Using grams or percents directly as subscripts. **Always convert to moles first.**
2. Dividing by something other than the **smallest mole value**, such as the smallest mass or the molar mass.
3. Rounding 1.5 to 2 or 1.33 to 1. Only round results within about 0.1 of a whole number.
4. Multiplying only the fractional element. **The same multiplier goes on every element.**
5. In Type C, multiplying only some of the subscripts by n.

# Chapter 9 — Chemical Quantities

## 9.0 How to read the worked examples in this chapter

Every Chapter 9 problem is a chain of **conversion factors**. A conversion factor is a fraction whose top and bottom are
equal amounts, so multiplying by it changes the **unit** without changing the **amount**. Only two kinds appear:

| Kind of factor | Where its numbers come from | Example |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Molar mass** (grams $\leftrightarrow$ moles) | Add up the atomic masses on the periodic table (section 8.5) | $\dfrac{58.44\ \text{g NaCl}}{1\ \text{mol NaCl}}$ |
| **Mole ratio** (moles of one substance $\leftrightarrow$ moles of another) | The **coefficients** of those two substances in the **balanced** equation | $\dfrac{2\ \text{mol NaCl}}{1\ \text{mol Cl}_2}$ |

**Orientation rule:** write the factor with the unit you **want** on top and the unit you **have** on the bottom. The unit
on the bottom cancels the unit you're carrying, and you're left with the unit on top. In the examples below, the labels
under each factor say where its numbers came from, and crossed-out units are the ones that cancel.

## 9.1 What a balanced equation tells you (Ch 9 slides 2–5)

* A balanced equation gives the **identities** of the reactants and products and **how much** of each takes part.
* **Coefficients give relative numbers of molecules (or moles), never grams.** What matters is the *ratio* of the
  coefficients, not any single coefficient.
* CO(g) + 2H~2~(g) $\rightarrow$ CH~3~OH(l) can be read as 1 molecule + 2 molecules $\rightarrow$ 1 molecule, as
  1 dozen + 2 dozen $\rightarrow$ 1 dozen, or as **1 mol + 2 mol $\rightarrow$ 1 mol** (Table 9.1).

**Worked example (slide 4).** 2Al~2~O~3~ $\rightarrow$ 4Al + 3O~2~. The coefficients are Al~2~O~3~ **2**, Al **4**, O~2~ **3**.

*(a) How many O~2~ molecules come from 4 molecules of Al~2~O~3~?* You have Al~2~O~3~ and want O~2~, so the factor is
(O~2~ coefficient) over (Al~2~O~3~ coefficient):

$$4\ \cancel{\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3} \times \underbrace{\frac{3\ \text{O}_2}{2\ \cancel{\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3}}}_{\text{coefficients of O}_2\text{ and Al}_2\text{O}_3} = \mathbf{6\ O_2\ molecules}$$

*(b) If 8 atoms of Al are produced, how many O~2~ molecules form?* You have Al and want O~2~:

$$8\ \cancel{\text{Al}} \times \underbrace{\frac{3\ \text{O}_2}{4\ \cancel{\text{Al}}}}_{\text{coefficients of O}_2\text{ and Al}} = \mathbf{6\ O_2\ molecules}$$

## 9.2 Mole ratios (Ch 9 slides 5–9)

A **mole ratio** comes from the coefficients of **two** substances in a balanced equation. Every pair of substances gives
one, and each one can be written right side up or upside down.

**How to build one.** From 2H~2~O $\rightarrow$ 2H~2~ + O~2~ (coefficients: H~2~O **2**, H~2~ **2**, O~2~ **1**):

| Pair | Statement | The two conversion factors it gives |
|:--|:--|:--|
| H~2~O and H~2~ | 2 mol H~2~O makes 2 mol H~2~ | $\dfrac{2\ \text{mol H}_2}{2\ \text{mol H}_2\text{O}}$ or $\dfrac{2\ \text{mol H}_2\text{O}}{2\ \text{mol H}_2}$ |
| H~2~O and O~2~ | 2 mol H~2~O makes 1 mol O~2~ | $\dfrac{1\ \text{mol O}_2}{2\ \text{mol H}_2\text{O}}$ or $\dfrac{2\ \text{mol H}_2\text{O}}{1\ \text{mol O}_2}$ |
| H~2~ and O~2~ | 2 mol H~2~ forms with 1 mol O~2~ | $\dfrac{1\ \text{mol O}_2}{2\ \text{mol H}_2}$ or $\dfrac{2\ \text{mol H}_2}{1\ \text{mol O}_2}$ |

**Which one to use:** the one with the substance you **want** on top and the substance you **have** on the bottom.
For 4B + 3O~2~ $\rightarrow$ 2B~2~O~3~, going from mol B to mol O~2~ uses $\dfrac{3\ \text{mol O}_2}{4\ \text{mol B}}$ (HW22).
The 3 is O~2~'s coefficient and the 4 is B's coefficient.

**Worked example (slide 7).** N~2~ + 3H~2~ $\rightarrow$ 2NH~3~ (coefficients N~2~ **1**, H~2~ **3**, NH~3~ **2**).
The mole ratios are 1 mol N~2~ : 3 mol H~2~, 1 mol N~2~ : 2 mol NH~3~, and 3 mol H~2~ : 2 mol NH~3~.

**Worked example (slide 8).** N~2~ + O~2~ $\rightarrow$ 2NO (coefficients N~2~ **1**, O~2~ **1**, NO **2**).
The mole ratios are 1 mol N~2~ : 1 mol O~2~, 1 mol N~2~ : 2 mol NO, and 1 mol O~2~ : 2 mol NO.

**Worked example (slide 9): balance first.** Ethane burns: C~2~H~6~ + O~2~ $\rightarrow$ CO~2~ + H~2~O.

1. **C:** 2 C on the left, so put 2 in front of CO~2~.
2. **H:** 6 H on the left, so put 3 in front of H~2~O (3 × 2 = 6 H).
3. **O:** the right now has 2(2) + 3(1) = 7 O, so O~2~ needs 7/2.
4. 7/2 isn't a whole number, so double **every** coefficient: **2C~2~H~6~ + 7O~2~ $\rightarrow$ 4CO~2~ + 6H~2~O**.

## 9.3 Mole–mole conversions (Ch 9 slides 10–12)

One step: multiply the moles you have by the mole ratio (want over have).

$$\text{mol wanted} = \text{mol given}\times\frac{\text{coefficient of the substance wanted}}{\text{coefficient of the substance given}}$$

**Worked example (slide 10).** Fe~2~O~3~ + 3CO $\rightarrow$ 2Fe + 3CO~2~. How many mol Fe form from 17.5 mol CO?
Have CO (coefficient **3**); want Fe (coefficient **2**).

$$17.5\ \cancel{\text{mol CO}} \times \underbrace{\frac{2\ \text{mol Fe}}{3\ \cancel{\text{mol CO}}}}_{\text{coefficients of Fe and CO}} = \mathbf{11.7\ mol\ Fe}$$

**Worked example (slide 11).** 2C~2~H~6~ + 7O~2~ $\rightarrow$ 4CO~2~ + 6H~2~O. How many mol O~2~ react with 0.987 mol C~2~H~6~?
Have C~2~H~6~ (coefficient **2**); want O~2~ (coefficient **7**).

$$0.987\ \cancel{\text{mol C}_2\text{H}_6} \times \underbrace{\frac{7\ \text{mol O}_2}{2\ \cancel{\text{mol C}_2\text{H}_6}}}_{\text{coefficients of O}_2\text{ and C}_2\text{H}_6} = \mathbf{3.45\ mol\ O_2}$$

**Worked example (slide 12).** NH~3~ + NaOCl $\rightarrow$ NaOH + NH~2~Cl. How much NH~2~Cl forms from 1.32 mol NH~3~?
Both coefficients are **1** (no number written means 1), so the ratio is 1 : 1.

$$1.32\ \cancel{\text{mol NH}_3} \times \underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol NH}_2\text{Cl}}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol NH}_3}}}_{\text{coefficients}} = 1.32\ \text{mol NH}_2\text{Cl}$$

To get grams, multiply by the molar mass of NH~2~Cl = 14.01 + 2(1.008) + 35.45 = 51.48 g/mol:

$$1.32\ \cancel{\text{mol NH}_2\text{Cl}} \times \underbrace{\frac{51.48\ \text{g NH}_2\text{Cl}}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol NH}_2\text{Cl}}}}_{\text{molar mass of NH}_2\text{Cl}} = \mathbf{67.9\ g\ NH_2Cl}$$

## 9.4 Stoichiometry with masses (Ch 9 slides 13–20)

**Stoichiometry:** using a balanced chemical equation to calculate the relative masses of reactants and products.
**The equation must be balanced first**, because the mole ratios come from the coefficients (slide 16).

**Steps (slide 14)**

1. Balance the equation.
2. Convert the grams you're given to **moles** (divide by that substance's molar mass).
3. Set up the **mole ratio** (want over have, from the coefficients).
4. Multiply to get the **moles** of the substance you want.
5. Convert those moles to **grams** (multiply by the wanted substance's molar mass).

$$\text{g A}\xrightarrow{\ \times\frac{1\ \text{mol A}}{\text{MM of A}}\ }\text{mol A}\xrightarrow{\ \times\frac{\text{coef B}}{\text{coef A}}\ }\text{mol B}\xrightarrow{\ \times\frac{\text{MM of B}}{1\ \text{mol B}}\ }\text{g B}$$

**You can never go straight from grams of A to grams of B.** The coefficients count moles, so you have to pass through moles.

**Worked example (slide 17).** 2SO~2~ + O~2~ $\rightarrow$ 2SO~3~. What mass of SO~3~ forms from 2.33 mol O~2~?

* **Given:** 2.33 mol O~2~. It's already in moles, so skip step 2.
* **Mole ratio:** have O~2~ (coefficient **1**), want SO~3~ (coefficient **2**).
* **Molar mass of SO~3~:** 32.07 + 3(16.00) = 80.07 g/mol.

$$2.33\ \cancel{\text{mol O}_2} \times \underbrace{\frac{2\ \text{mol SO}_3}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol O}_2}}}_{\text{coefficients}} = 4.66\ \text{mol SO}_3$$

$$4.66\ \cancel{\text{mol SO}_3} \times \underbrace{\frac{80.07\ \text{g SO}_3}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol SO}_3}}}_{\text{molar mass of SO}_3} = \mathbf{373\ g\ SO_3}$$

**Worked example (slide 18).** H~2~SO~4~ + 2KOH $\rightarrow$ K~2~SO~4~ + 2H~2~O. How many moles of H~2~SO~4~ react with 19.9 g KOH?

* **Molar mass of KOH:** 39.10 + 16.00 + 1.008 = 56.11 g/mol.
* **Mole ratio:** have KOH (coefficient **2**), want H~2~SO~4~ (coefficient **1**).
* The question asks for **moles**, so stop after the mole ratio (no step 5).

$$19.9\ \cancel{\text{g KOH}} \times \underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol KOH}}{56.11\ \cancel{\text{g KOH}}}}_{\text{molar mass of KOH}} = 0.3547\ \text{mol KOH}$$

$$0.3547\ \cancel{\text{mol KOH}} \times \underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol H}_2\text{SO}_4}{2\ \cancel{\text{mol KOH}}}}_{\text{coefficients}} = \mathbf{0.177\ mol\ H_2SO_4}$$

**Worked example (slide 19).** 4NH~3~ + 5O~2~ $\rightarrow$ 4NO + 6H~2~O. What mass of NH~3~ is needed to make 54.7 g NO?

* **Molar masses:** NO = 14.01 + 16.00 = 30.01 g/mol; NH~3~ = 14.01 + 3(1.008) = 17.03 g/mol.
* **Mole ratio:** have NO (coefficient **4**), want NH~3~ (coefficient **4**). It's 4 : 4, so the moles are equal.

$$54.7\ \cancel{\text{g NO}} \times \underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol NO}}{30.01\ \cancel{\text{g NO}}}}_{\text{molar mass of NO}} = 1.823\ \text{mol NO}$$

$$1.823\ \cancel{\text{mol NO}} \times \underbrace{\frac{4\ \text{mol NH}_3}{4\ \cancel{\text{mol NO}}}}_{\text{coefficients}} \times \underbrace{\frac{17.03\ \text{g NH}_3}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol NH}_3}}}_{\text{molar mass of NH}_3} = \mathbf{31.0\ g\ NH_3}$$

**Worked example (slide 20).** CuSO~4~ + Fe $\rightarrow$ FeSO~4~ + Cu. What mass of CuSO~4~ reacts with 244 g Fe?

* **Molar masses:** Fe = 55.85 g/mol; CuSO~4~ = 63.55 + 32.07 + 4(16.00) = 159.62 g/mol.
* **Mole ratio:** have Fe (coefficient **1**), want CuSO~4~ (coefficient **1**).

$$244\ \cancel{\text{g Fe}} \times \underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol Fe}}{55.85\ \cancel{\text{g Fe}}}}_{\text{molar mass of Fe}} = 4.369\ \text{mol Fe}$$

$$4.369\ \cancel{\text{mol Fe}} \times \underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol CuSO}_4}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol Fe}}}}_{\text{coefficients}} \times \underbrace{\frac{159.62\ \text{g CuSO}_4}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol CuSO}_4}}}_{\text{molar mass of CuSO}_4} = \mathbf{697\ g\ CuSO_4}$$

**HW23 style (balance first, work in mg).** Fe + Cl~2~ $\rightarrow$ FeCl~3~. What mass of FeCl~3~ forms from 20.5 mg Fe?

1. **Balance:** FeCl~3~ has 3 Cl, and Cl~2~ comes in pairs, so use 2FeCl~3~ (6 Cl) and 3Cl~2~ (6 Cl). Then 2 Fe on the
   left: **2Fe + 3Cl~2~ $\rightarrow$ 2FeCl~3~**.
2. **Molar masses:** Fe = 55.85; FeCl~3~ = 55.85 + 3(35.45) = 162.20. A molar mass in g/mol is the same number in
   **mg/mmol** (both top and bottom are divided by 1000), so you can stay in mg and mmol.
3. **Mole ratio:** have Fe (coefficient **2**), want FeCl~3~ (coefficient **2**).

$$20.5\ \cancel{\text{mg Fe}} \times \underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mmol Fe}}{55.85\ \cancel{\text{mg Fe}}}}_{\text{molar mass of Fe}} \times \underbrace{\frac{2\ \text{mmol FeCl}_3}{2\ \cancel{\text{mmol Fe}}}}_{\text{coefficients}} \times \underbrace{\frac{162.20\ \text{mg FeCl}_3}{1\ \cancel{\text{mmol FeCl}_3}}}_{\text{molar mass of FeCl}_3} = \mathbf{59.5\ mg\ FeCl_3}$$

## 9.5 Limiting reactant (Ch 9 slides 21–24)

* **Limiting reactant (limiting reagent):** the reactant that is **used up first**. It **controls how much product forms**.
* The other reactant is **in excess**: some of it is left over.

**Method**

1. Convert every reactant to **moles**.
2. Pick one reactant. Use the mole ratio to find **how many moles of the other reactant it needs** to react completely.
3. Compare that **need** with what you **have** of the other reactant:
   * have **more** than needed: the other reactant is in excess, so the one you picked is **limiting**;
   * have **less** than needed: the other reactant runs out first, so **it** is limiting.

**Cross-check (optional):** calculate how many moles of product each reactant could make on its own. The reactant that
gives the **smaller** amount is limiting.

**Never compare grams, and never compare raw mole amounts without the mole ratio.** A reactant with more moles can
still be limiting if the equation needs a lot of it.

**Worked example (slide 23).** 3Mg + N~2~ $\rightarrow$ Mg~3~N~2~, with 4.75 mol Mg and 2.11 mol N~2~. Which is limiting?

*Step 1:* both are already in moles.

*Step 2:* pick Mg and find how much N~2~ it needs. Have Mg (coefficient **3**), want N~2~ (coefficient **1**):

$$4.75\ \cancel{\text{mol Mg}} \times \underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol N}_2}{3\ \cancel{\text{mol Mg}}}}_{\text{coefficients of N}_2\text{ and Mg}} = 1.58\ \text{mol N}_2\ \text{needed}$$

*Step 3:* you **have** 2.11 mol N~2~ but only **need** 1.58 mol. There's more N~2~ than the Mg can use, so N~2~ is in
excess and **Mg is limiting**. (Note that Mg has *more* moles, 4.75 vs 2.11, and is still limiting, because the equation
uses 3 Mg for every 1 N~2~.)

**Worked example (slide 24).** 4Al + 3O~2~ $\rightarrow$ 2Al~2~O~3~, with 17.9 g Al and 64 g O~2~. Which is limiting?

*Step 1: grams to moles.* Molar masses: Al = 26.98 g/mol; O~2~ = 2(16.00) = 32.00 g/mol (O~2~ has two O atoms).

$$17.9\ \cancel{\text{g Al}} \times \underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol Al}}{26.98\ \cancel{\text{g Al}}}}_{\text{molar mass of Al}} = 0.6635\ \text{mol Al}$$

$$64\ \cancel{\text{g O}_2} \times \underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol O}_2}{32.00\ \cancel{\text{g O}_2}}}_{\text{molar mass of O}_2} = 2.0\ \text{mol O}_2$$

*Step 2:* pick Al and find how much O~2~ it needs. Have Al (coefficient **4**), want O~2~ (coefficient **3**):

$$0.6635\ \cancel{\text{mol Al}} \times \underbrace{\frac{3\ \text{mol O}_2}{4\ \cancel{\text{mol Al}}}}_{\text{coefficients of O}_2\text{ and Al}} = 0.498\ \text{mol O}_2\ \text{needed}$$

*Step 3:* you **have** 2.0 mol O~2~ and only **need** 0.498 mol, so O~2~ is in excess and **Al is limiting**. Al also has
the smaller mass here, but that is *not* the reason. The comparison has to be made in moles through the mole ratio.

## 9.6 Theoretical yield (Ch 9 slides 25–27)

**Theoretical yield:** the amount of product **calculated from the limiting reactant**. It is the **maximum** amount of product
that can be made from the amounts of reactants used.

**Method**

1. Find the **limiting reactant** (section 9.5). If the problem says one reactant is "in excess," the **other** one is limiting.
2. Start from the **moles of the limiting reactant**. Never start from the excess reactant.
3. Multiply by the mole ratio $\dfrac{\text{coefficient of the product}}{\text{coefficient of the limiting reactant}}$ to get moles of product.
4. Multiply by the **molar mass of the product** to get grams of product. That number is the theoretical yield.

**Worked example (slide 26): one reactant in excess.** Pb(NO~3~)~2~ + 2NaCl $\rightarrow$ PbCl~2~ + 2NaNO~3~, with 237 g NaCl
and excess Pb(NO~3~)~2~. What is the theoretical yield of PbCl~2~?

*Step 1: limiting reactant.* Pb(NO~3~)~2~ is "in excess," which means there's more than enough of it. So **NaCl is limiting**,
and no comparison is needed.

*Step 2: grams NaCl to moles NaCl.* Molar mass of NaCl = 22.99 + 35.45 = 58.44 g/mol.

$$237\ \cancel{\text{g NaCl}} \times \underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol NaCl}}{58.44\ \cancel{\text{g NaCl}}}}_{\text{molar mass of NaCl}} = 4.055\ \text{mol NaCl}$$

*Step 3: moles NaCl to moles PbCl~2~.* In the balanced equation, NaCl's coefficient is **2** and PbCl~2~'s coefficient is
**1**. So 2 mol NaCl makes 1 mol PbCl~2~. Want PbCl~2~ on top, have NaCl on the bottom:

$$4.055\ \cancel{\text{mol NaCl}} \times \underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol PbCl}_2}{2\ \cancel{\text{mol NaCl}}}}_{\text{coefficient of PbCl}_2\ /\ \text{coefficient of NaCl}} = 2.028\ \text{mol PbCl}_2$$

*Step 4: moles PbCl~2~ to grams PbCl~2~.* Molar mass of PbCl~2~ = 207.2 + 2(35.45) = 278.1 g/mol.

$$2.028\ \cancel{\text{mol PbCl}_2} \times \underbrace{\frac{278.1\ \text{g PbCl}_2}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol PbCl}_2}}}_{\text{molar mass of PbCl}_2} = \mathbf{564\ g\ PbCl_2}\ \text{(theoretical yield)}$$

**Worked example (slide 27): you have to find the limiting reactant first.** 2Na + Cl~2~ $\rightarrow$ 2NaCl, with
68 g Na and 97 g Cl~2~. What is the theoretical yield of NaCl?

*Read the equation first.* Coefficients: Na **2**, Cl~2~ **1**, NaCl **2**. In words: 2 mol Na reacts with 1 mol Cl~2~
to make 2 mol NaCl. The three mole ratios you can use are:

$$\frac{2\ \text{mol Na}}{1\ \text{mol Cl}_2} \qquad \frac{2\ \text{mol NaCl}}{2\ \text{mol Na}} \qquad \frac{2\ \text{mol NaCl}}{1\ \text{mol Cl}_2}$$

*Step 1a: grams to moles for each reactant.* Molar masses: Na = 22.99 g/mol (periodic table); Cl~2~ = 2(35.45) =
70.90 g/mol (Cl~2~ is diatomic, so it has **two** Cl atoms).

$$68\ \cancel{\text{g Na}} \times \underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol Na}}{22.99\ \cancel{\text{g Na}}}}_{\text{molar mass of Na}} = 2.958\ \text{mol Na}$$

$$97\ \cancel{\text{g Cl}_2} \times \underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol Cl}_2}{70.90\ \cancel{\text{g Cl}_2}}}_{\text{molar mass of Cl}_2} = 1.368\ \text{mol Cl}_2$$

*Step 1b: how much Na does all the Cl~2~ need?* Have Cl~2~ (coefficient **1**), want Na (coefficient **2**):

$$1.368\ \cancel{\text{mol Cl}_2} \times \underbrace{\frac{2\ \text{mol Na}}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol Cl}_2}}}_{\text{coefficient of Na}\ /\ \text{coefficient of Cl}_2} = 2.736\ \text{mol Na needed}$$

*Step 1c: compare.* You **have** 2.958 mol Na and the Cl~2~ only **needs** 2.736 mol Na. There's extra Na (2.958 − 2.736 =
0.222 mol left over), so Na is in excess and the Cl~2~ runs out first: **Cl~2~ is limiting**.

*Step 2: start from the limiting reactant, 1.368 mol Cl~2~.*

*Step 3: moles Cl~2~ to moles NaCl.* Have Cl~2~ (coefficient **1**), want NaCl (coefficient **2**). Here the 2 is
**NaCl's** coefficient, not Na's. They happen to be the same number in this equation.

$$1.368\ \cancel{\text{mol Cl}_2} \times \underbrace{\frac{2\ \text{mol NaCl}}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol Cl}_2}}}_{\text{coefficient of NaCl}\ /\ \text{coefficient of Cl}_2} = 2.736\ \text{mol NaCl}$$

*Step 4: moles NaCl to grams NaCl.* Molar mass of NaCl = 22.99 (Na) + 35.45 (Cl) = 58.44 g/mol.

$$2.736\ \cancel{\text{mol NaCl}} \times \underbrace{\frac{58.44\ \text{g NaCl}}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol NaCl}}}}_{\text{molar mass of NaCl}} = \mathbf{160\ g\ NaCl}\ \text{(theoretical yield)}$$

*All of steps 2–4 as one chain:*

$$97\ \cancel{\text{g Cl}_2}\times\frac{1\ \cancel{\text{mol Cl}_2}}{70.90\ \cancel{\text{g Cl}_2}}\times\frac{2\ \cancel{\text{mol NaCl}}}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol Cl}_2}}\times\frac{58.44\ \text{g NaCl}}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol NaCl}}} = 160\ \text{g NaCl}$$

*Check with the cross-check method.* If all the Na reacted, it would make
2.958 mol Na × (2 mol NaCl / 2 mol Na) × 58.44 g/mol = 173 g NaCl. That's more than the 160 g the Cl~2~ allows, and the
**smaller** amount wins. Using the Na would give 173 g, a wrong answer that is likely to appear among the choices, because
there isn't enough Cl~2~ to make that much.

## 9.7 Actual and percent yield (Ch 9 slides 28–32)

* **Actual yield:** the amount of product **actually produced**. It is usually less than the theoretical yield, for example
  because of **side reactions** that consume reactants or products.
* **Percent yield** shows how efficient a reaction is:

$$\text{percent yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}}\times100\%$$

* The **actual yield is given** in the problem (it was measured). The **theoretical yield you calculate** (section 9.6). Both
  must be in the same unit, usually grams.
* **Can the actual yield be higher than the theoretical yield (slide 29)?** No. The theoretical yield is the maximum. A
  result over 100% means an error, such as a wet or impure product or a math mistake.

**Worked example (slide 31).** H~2~ + I~2~ $\rightarrow$ 2HI, with 69.1 g H~2~ and excess I~2~. 134 g HI is actually produced.
What is the percent yield?

*Part 1: theoretical yield of HI.* I~2~ is in excess, so **H~2~ is limiting**. Molar masses: H~2~ = 2(1.008) = 2.016 g/mol;
HI = 1.008 + 126.90 = 127.91 g/mol. Mole ratio: have H~2~ (coefficient **1**), want HI (coefficient **2**).

$$69.1\ \cancel{\text{g H}_2} \times \underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol H}_2}{2.016\ \cancel{\text{g H}_2}}}_{\text{molar mass of H}_2} = 34.28\ \text{mol H}_2$$

$$34.28\ \cancel{\text{mol H}_2} \times \underbrace{\frac{2\ \text{mol HI}}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol H}_2}}}_{\text{coefficients}} \times \underbrace{\frac{127.91\ \text{g HI}}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol HI}}}}_{\text{molar mass of HI}} = 8768\ \text{g HI (theoretical)}$$

*Part 2: percent yield.* The actual yield (134 g) goes on top and the theoretical yield (8768 g) on the bottom:

$$\frac{134\ \text{g}}{8768\ \text{g}}\times100\% = \mathbf{1.53\%}$$

**Worked example (slide 32).** 2KClO~3~ $\rightarrow$ 2KCl + 3O~2~, with 191 g KClO~3~. 89.9 g KCl is actually produced.
What is the percent yield?

*Part 1: theoretical yield of KCl.* KClO~3~ is the only reactant, so it's limiting. Molar masses: KClO~3~ = 39.10 + 35.45 +
3(16.00) = 122.55 g/mol; KCl = 39.10 + 35.45 = 74.55 g/mol. Mole ratio: have KClO~3~ (coefficient **2**), want KCl
(coefficient **2**).

$$191\ \cancel{\text{g KClO}_3} \times \underbrace{\frac{1\ \text{mol KClO}_3}{122.55\ \cancel{\text{g KClO}_3}}}_{\text{molar mass of KClO}_3} = 1.559\ \text{mol KClO}_3$$

$$1.559\ \cancel{\text{mol KClO}_3} \times \underbrace{\frac{2\ \text{mol KCl}}{2\ \cancel{\text{mol KClO}_3}}}_{\text{coefficients}} \times \underbrace{\frac{74.55\ \text{g KCl}}{1\ \cancel{\text{mol KCl}}}}_{\text{molar mass of KCl}} = 116.2\ \text{g KCl (theoretical)}$$

*Part 2: percent yield.*

$$\frac{89.9\ \text{g}}{116.2\ \text{g}}\times100\% = \mathbf{77.4\%}$$

**HW24 style (two-part).** Some problems give amounts of **both** reactants (for example Xe + 2F~2~ $\rightarrow$ XeF~4~). Then
part 1 needs the limiting reactant first (section 9.5), followed by the theoretical yield from that reactant (section 9.6).
Part 2 is percent yield = actual / theoretical × 100. "Percentage of capacity reached" (the LiOH and CO~2~ canister) uses the
same formula: actual / theoretical × 100.

\newpage

# Common traps — check these before you bubble

1. **Solubility exceptions:** AgCl, PbCl~2~, Hg~2~Cl~2~ and BaSO~4~, PbSO~4~, CaSO~4~ are insoluble. Na^+^/K^+^/NH~4~^+^/NO~3~^−^ always win.
2. **Net ionic means no spectators.** A choice that still has Na^+^ and NO~3~^−^ on both sides is the complete ionic equation.
3. **Precipitates are (s).** The same formula labeled (aq) is a wrong choice.
4. **Strong acids are HCl, HNO~3~, H~2~SO~4~ only.** HNO~2~ $\neq$ HNO~3~.
5. **Electrons per atom = ion charge**, not the total for the equation.
6. **More than one class can apply.** A single replacement is also redox. Burning in O~2~ is combustion even when one product forms.
7. **mg $\rightarrow$ g first.** 1 mg = 10^−3^ g and 1 $\mu$g = 10^−6^ g.
8. **Subscripts outside parentheses multiply everything inside**: Al~2~(SO~4~)~3~ has 12 O.
9. **Mass percent uses mass, not atom counts.** 1 P out of 8 atoms is not 12.5% P.
10. **Empirical formula:** divide by the *smallest* number of moles; multiply to clear 0.5, 0.33, or 0.25 fractions.
11. **Coefficients are moles, not grams.** Always convert to moles before using a ratio.
12. **Limiting reactant:** compare moles needed with moles available. Never compare grams or coefficients alone.
13. **Percent yield $\leq$ 100%.** Divide actual by **theoretical** yield, not by the mass of the reactant.

# Glossary of course definitions

| Term | Course definition (slide) |
|:--|:--|
| Precipitation / precipitate | Formation of a solid when two solutions are mixed; the solid is the precipitate (7: 5, 35) |
| Strong electrolyte | Each unit that dissolves produces separated ions (7: 7) |
| Molecular equation | Shows complete formulas of all reactants and products (7: 15) |
| Complete ionic equation | All strong electrolytes shown as ions; all reactants and products included (7: 16, 18) |
| Net ionic equation | Only the components directly involved / that undergo a change; no spectators (7: 17) |
| Spectator ions | Ions that don't participate directly in the reaction (7: 17) |
| Arrhenius acid / base | Produces H^+^ / OH^−^ in water (7: 21, 22) |
| Strong acid | Completely dissociates (ionizes) in water: HCl, HNO~3~, H~2~SO~4~ (7: 24) |
| Strong base | Metal hydroxide that is very soluble and completely breaks into ions: NaOH, KOH (7: 25) |
| Salt | Ionic compound formed with water in an acid–base reaction (7: 23, 26) |
| Oxidation–reduction | Reaction involving a transfer of electrons (7: 30) |
| Double-displacement | Two anions exchanged between cations (7: 36) |
| Single-replacement | One anion moves from one cation to another (7: 40) |
| Combustion | Reaction with oxygen that releases energy fast enough to make a flame (7: 41) |
| Synthesis (combination) | A compound forms from simpler materials (7: 42) |
| Decomposition | A compound breaks into simpler compounds or elements, by heat or current (7: 43) |
| Atomic mass unit | 1 amu = 1.66 × 10^−24^ g (8: 5) |
| Mole | Number of C atoms in 12.01 g of C = 6.022 × 10^23^ (Avogadro's number) (8: 7) |
| Molar mass | Mass in grams of 1 mole of a substance; sum of the atomic masses (8: 22) |
| Mass percent | (Mass of element in 1 mol) / (mass of 1 mol) × 100% (8: 30) |
| Empirical formula | Smallest whole-number ratio of atoms (8: 39) |
| Molecular formula | Actual formula = (empirical)~n~ (8: 39, 48) |
| Stoichiometry | Using a balanced equation to calculate masses of reactants and products (9: 15) |
| Limiting reactant | The reactant used up first; it controls the amount of product (9: 21) |
| Theoretical yield | Product amount calculated from the limiting reactant; the maximum possible (9: 25, 28) |
| Actual yield | Product amount actually obtained (9: 28) |
| Percent yield | Actual / theoretical × 100% (9: 30) |
